title: Training Quantum Self-Attention Model in Near-Term Quantum Computer
journal_or_venue: 16th International Conference on Wireless Communications and Signal Processing (IEEE)
abstract_summary: This paper proposes and implements a quantum self-attention model trained directly on a NISQ-era superconducting 72-qubit quantum computer ("Wukong"). It introduces circuit design optimizations and three levels of parallel training strategies to mitigate noise and accelerate training, and demonstrates feasibility on two NLP benchmarks (MC and RP), reporting that models trained on real hardware achieve competitive — and in some cases slightly better — performance than simulators.
methodology_description: The authors design and implement a variational quantum self-attention model for sentence / phrase classification and train it directly on a NISQ superconducting quantum processor. Classical token vectors are first compressed by element-wise arctan and encoded into quantum states via single-qubit rotation gates. For each token three parameterized variational quantum circuits (VQCs) produce query (Q), key (K) and value (V) vectors: Q and K circuits are measured via single-qubit expectation values while the V circuit measures all qubits. The classical self-attention operation (softmax(QK^T) V) is then applied to produce token representations, followed by a classical loss computation. Gradients for the VQC parameters are obtained using the parameter-shift rule and parameters are updated by a classical optimizer (gradient-descent style update). To reduce wall-clock time on hardware the authors propose and employ three levels of parallelism (attention-level, token-level, batch-level) and implement a multi-way parallel scheme on the chip. The variational circuit ansatz uses alternating layers of single-qubit parameterized rotation gates and CZ entangling gates (odd/even layering). Experiments compare runs on a simulator vs runs on the OriginQ 'Wukong' 72-qubit superconducting quantum computer; datasets are two small NLP classification corpora (MC and RP). Training and evaluation metrics (loss, accuracy) are reported over epochs and hardware runtime (forward/backward propagation time) is profiled.
algorithms_used: Quantum self-attention model (quantum analog of Q/K/V)
experimental_setup: Runs performed on OriginQ 'Wukong' 72-qubit superconducting quantum processor (used a 28-qubit, seven-way parallel allocation) and compared to a software simulator. Hardware reported single-qubit gate fidelity ~0.9969, CZ fidelity ~0.9637, T1 ≈ 14.78 µs, T2 ≈ 1.87 µs. Each quantum circuit executed ~2000 shots; authors report per-circuit effective time ≈ 0.2 s after sampling and queue/communication overhead. Topology groups of qubits selected according to chip diagram; experiments submitted via a quantum cloud runtime.

results_summary: The paper reports the practical training of a variational quantum self-attention model directly on a 72-qubit superconducting quantum computer (Wukong). Using two small binary text classification benchmarks (MC and RP), the authors obtained perfect accuracy on MC and higher test accuracy on RP using hardware (83.88%) than their simulator (80.66%). They describe circuit design choices (encoding, alternating CZ layers), use the parameter-shift rule for gradients, and run many shots per circuit (2000). The work also presents theoretical parallelism strategies to speed up VQC evaluation and reports measured device fidelities and per-step timings (forward ≈85 s, backward ≈270 s). The paper emphasizes feasibility of running small NLP models on NISQ hardware but does not claim a classical or provable quantum advantage.

key_ideas: #idea:near-term-feasibility — Demonstrates end-to-end training of a variational quantum self-attention model directly on a superconducting NISQ device (OriginQ 'Wukong'), using a 28-qubit allocation and reporting competitive test accuracies on two small NLP datasets.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Uses classical preprocessing (element-wise arctan compression), classical softmax and loss computation, and classical optimizers with parameter-shift gradients while quantum VQCs produce Q/K/V vectors (hybrid QPU-CPU training loop).
#idea:hybrid-approach — Introduces three levels of parallelism (attention-level, token-level, batch-level) to reduce wall-clock hardware time and implements multi-way parallel execution on-chip.

#limitation:qubit-count — Experiments use 28 active qubits (seven-way parallel) on a 72-qubit processor and very small datasets (<=130 sentences), indicating limited scale and uncertain applicability to larger, finance-sized problems.

#limitation:noise — Hardware noise characteristics (CZ fidelity ~0.9637, T2 ~1.87 μs) are explicitly reported; authors apply circuit design and parallel-training strategies to mitigate but noise remains a constraint for deeper circuits and longer sequences.

#limitation:data-encoding — Classical token vectors are compressed via arctan and encoded with single-qubit rotations; this explicit encoding choice may limit representational capacity and raises questions about cost/accuracy trade-offs for richer financial data.
contradictions: Paper reports hardware test accuracy exceeding simulator on the RP dataset (hardware 83.88% vs simulator 80.66%), which runs counter to the expectation that noise-free simulators should at least match or outperform noisy NISQ hardware. This raises questions about simulator configuration, dataset variability, or stochastic effects in measurement.

Authors report dramatically lower wall-clock times on hardware versus simulator estimates (hardware forward/backward steps << simulator estimates). This may contradict assumptions about classical simulation speed for small circuits but could reflect differences in simulator implementation/optimisation rather than an inherent quantum runtime advantage.
